notes: Safety-critical file. This dictionary is the only thing the app uses to decide whether an ingredient carries an allergen or restricted-food tag. Unknown ingredients are reported as unknown, never as safe (PHASE-2 section 5, rule 10).

match semantics: 'word' = whole-word, case-insensitive, matches the singular and simple plural (s, es, y->ies) of the last word; multi-word terms are allowed and match with word boundaries. 'phrase' = the exact phrase with word boundaries, no plural. 'substring' = anywhere inside a token; used only for tokens that are unambiguous inside longer words (casein, lactalbumin, phosph).

Normalization before matching: lowercase; apostrophes removed; hyphens and slashes become spaces; whitespace collapsed. Terms in this file are normalized the same way, so 'high-fructose corn syrup' and 'high fructose corn syrup' are the same term.

except: if a match falls inside one of the listed longer phrases, this entry does not fire (e.g. 'butter' does not fire inside 'peanut butter'; 'milk' does not fire inside 'coconut milk'). The longer phrase has its own entry where it carries tags. Except phrases are matched with the same 'word' rules (plural allowed on the last word). An engine that ignores 'except' over-flags, which is the safe direction.

may_contain: tags the ingredient frequently but not always carries (sausage: gluten, lactose-hidden). The checker must show 'verify label' when the person's plan restricts one of these tags and must never count the ingredient as passing. It must not treat may_contain as a confirmed match either.

Unknown-risk contract: an entry with tags [] is a recognized label term that can hide allergens or whose composition the name does not settle (natural flavors, spices, seasoning, hydrolyzed vegetable protein, oyster sauce, tortilla, cider, vegetable broth). Every such entry also carries risk: 'unknown' for readability; src/engine/dictionary.js keys unknown-risk on the empty tag list. The checker reports these as unknown-risk and, when an allergen is selected, as caution or hard fail per PHASE-2 section 5 rule 1. Terms that were reviewed and deliberately left untagged are NOT entries; they are recorded under not_tagged so they fall through as 'not recognized'.

Allergen tags are conservative by design: when a name is ambiguous (mixed nuts, shellfish, coconut, chestnut, goat milk, peanut oil, almond extract) the tag is kept and the note explains. The allergist decides what to relax.

Tree nut list: FDA's allergen guidance, Edition 5 (January 2025; 90 FR 1133), Table 1, lists 12 tree nuts as major food allergens: almond, black walnut, Brazil nut, California walnut, cashew, filbert or hazelnut, heartnut or Japanese walnut, macadamia or bush nut, pecan, pine nut, pistachio, and walnut. Coconut, chestnut, and other nuts on the earlier list were removed; the guidance (C.8) says tree nuts not in Table 1 must still be named in the ingredient list but not in the "Contains" statement. This dictionary keeps the tree nut tag on coconut (every coconut product: milk, cream, water, oil, flour, sugar, aminos), chestnut, and any unnamed "nut" on purpose: the tag is a hard exclusion, and the app has no hard way for one person to add a single food, so dropping it would leave anyone who reacts to them with only a soft "words to avoid" caution. Checked September 30, 2026 (VERIFY-log item 8).

FODMAP tags are not Monash-app-verified. They come from the published Monash-group composition studies (Muir 2007, Muir 2009, Biesiekierski 2011), the Halmos 2014 trial food lists, and the Varney 2017 cut-off paper. Where a food is known to have a low-FODMAP portion only from the Monash app, no FODMAP tag is assigned and the food is listed under 'unsure'. No numeric portion thresholds are encoded; portion_note says so.

Histamine tags rest on patient-reported and food-chemistry evidence (Comas-Baste 2020, Reese 2017, SIGHI list, AGA 2025 hEDS update). Not RCT-confirmed. Freshness and storage matter more than the food name; the 'leftovers' entry carries that rule. The 'histamine liberator' foods (citrus, strawberry, chocolate, some nuts) are contested and are tagged because Phase 1 Part A 7 lists them as commonly reported triggers.

Kidney tags never set a limit. potassium-high-food entries are the classic clinician list and apply only when serum potassium is high (KDIGO 2024, KDOQI 2020). Phosphate additives are the priority over natural phosphorus.
Oxalate: the pairing rule is to eat high-oxalate foods with a calcium source in the same meal rather than eliminating them, and never to restrict calcium (AUA 2014/2019).

Purine tags follow the ACR 2020 framing (organ meats, certain seafood, alcohol, HFCS) and Choi 2004 for meat versus seafood versus vegetable purines. Phase 1 A7 lists shellfish among purine-rich foods, so crustaceans and mollusks are tagged purine-high. Purine-rich vegetables and legumes are not tagged.

Pregnancy food-safety tags follow FDA/FoodSafety.gov and ACOG. Soft cheeses carry 'unless labeled pasteurized'. Deli meats and hot dogs are safe when heated until steaming. Mercury tiers follow FDA/EPA 2021; only 'Choices to Avoid' and 'Best Choices' have tags, 'Good Choices' are noted (see proposed_tags).

Pattern tags (vegetable, fruit, whole-grain, and so on) are used by prefer rules and by USDA food auto-tagging. They are not safety tags. The curated overrides file (tools/food-tags.json) reviews what the dictionary assigns to USDA foods.

Texture tags are recipe-level hints for gastroparesis and IBD flare. The dictionary cannot know whether a vegetable is cooked or raw; it tags foods that are usually eaten raw and explicit 'raw X' phrases.

Per-entry 'sources' are given for the evidence-sensitive families (FODMAP, histamine, oxalate, purine, potassium, mercury, pregnancy). Where an entry has no 'sources', the tag declaration's sources apply.

Words that are ambiguous between an allergen and an unrelated food are handled by the except list, not by weakening the tag: 'kidney' (organ) versus 'kidney bean', 'egg' versus 'eggplant' (word boundary), 'butternut' is not in the dictionary at all because it is not a common food ingredient and would collide with butternut squash.

Brand names are included only where they are used as generic ingredient words in US recipes (Splenda, Truvia, Velveeta, Spam, Tums, Marmite, Vegemite, Kahlua, Cointreau, Grand Marnier, Frappuccino, Sunbutter).

Sept 5, 2026: declared the 14 tags used by conditions.json rules (may-contain, GERD and migraine optional triggers, tea, iron-rich, vitamin-c-rich, emulsifier-additive, smoked-seafood-refrigerated) and added entries. Trigger tags drive optional toggles only; they are never default exclusions. Lecithin, xanthan gum, guar gum and maltodextrin carry emulsifier-additive only as label markers for the IBD remission ultra-processed guidance.
Sept 5, 2026: added basic-ingredient tag so common pantry words (salt, water, spices, starches, plain oils) are recognized rather than reported as unknown. Vinegars keep their fermented tag.

allergen-milk.label: Milk
allergen-milk.description: Cow's milk and every milk-derived ingredient (whey, casein, butter, cream, cheese, and so on). Hard exclusion. Plant 'milks' are excluded from the match by name where the dictionary lists them.

allergen-egg.label: Egg
allergen-egg.description: Hen's egg and egg-derived ingredients (albumin, ovalbumin, lysozyme, mayonnaise, meringue). Hard exclusion.

allergen-fish.label: Fish
allergen-fish.description: Finfish of any species and fish-derived ingredients (fish sauce, fish oil, surimi, anchovy paste). Hard exclusion. Mollusks (oyster, clam, squid) are not an FDA major allergen; they carry a note, not this tag.

allergen-crustacean.label: Crustacean shellfish
allergen-crustacean.description: Shrimp, prawn, crab, lobster, crayfish, langoustine, krill and their derivatives. Hard exclusion. The generic term 'shellfish' is tagged conservatively.

allergen-tree-nut.label: Tree nut
allergen-tree-nut.description: Almond, Brazil nut, cashew, hazelnut (filbert), heartnut (Japanese walnut), macadamia, pecan, pine nut, pistachio, and walnut (including black and California walnut), and their derivatives: FDA's 12 tree nuts (Edition 5, January 2025). Hard exclusion. Coconut and chestnut are also tagged, on purpose, although FDA removed them in 2025: the app cannot tell who reacts to them.

allergen-peanut.label: Peanut
allergen-peanut.description: Peanut and peanut-derived ingredients (groundnut, arachis oil, peanut flour). Hard exclusion. Highly refined peanut oil is exempt from FALCPA labeling but is tagged conservatively.

allergen-wheat.label: Wheat
allergen-wheat.description: Wheat in all species (common, durum, spelt, kamut, einkorn, emmer, semolina, triticale) and wheat-derived ingredients. Hard exclusion. Distinct from the gluten tag: rye and barley are gluten but not wheat.

allergen-soy.label: Soy
allergen-soy.description: Soybeans and soy protein foods (tofu, edamame, miso, soy sauce, TVP). Hard exclusion. Highly refined soybean oil (soy-refined-oil) is exempt from FALCPA labeling; soy lecithin (soy-lecithin) is not exempt and is declared as soy. Both carry their own tags; the allergy module excludes them by default and lets the user relax that with allergist input.

allergen-sesame.label: Sesame
allergen-sesame.description: Sesame seed and sesame-derived ingredients (tahini, benne, gingelly, halvah, sesame oil). Hard exclusion; ninth major allergen under the FASTER Act.

gluten.label: Gluten
gluten.description: Contains gluten from wheat, barley, rye, or triticale, or a derivative of them. Excluded for celiac disease and gluten-free patterns.

gluten-hidden.label: Hidden gluten
gluten-hidden.description: Gluten present in an ingredient whose name does not say wheat, barley, or rye (soy sauce, malt vinegar, brewer's yeast, communion wafer). Always paired with the gluten tag. Ingredients that only sometimes contain gluten are not tagged; they carry gluten in their may_contain list instead.

oats-regular.label: Oats, not certified gluten-free
oats-regular.description: Oats without a gluten-free label. Oats do not contain gluten but are routinely cross-contaminated with wheat and barley in the field and mill; flagged for celiac disease.

oats-certified-gf.label: Oats, labeled gluten-free
oats-certified-gf.description: Oats labeled gluten-free (under 20 ppm). Safe for most people with celiac disease per ACG 2023; a small subset react to oat avenin, so the app offers a toggle to exclude them.

soy.label: Soy food
soy.description: Soy as a food ingredient (soybeans, tofu, soy milk, soy protein). Used by the soy-free preference and by the levothyroxine timing rule. Not itself a hard exclusion; allergen-soy is.

soy-refined-oil.label: Refined soybean oil
soy-refined-oil.description: Highly refined soybean oil. Exempt from FALCPA labeling; tolerated by most people with soy allergy. The allergy module excludes it by default and lets the user relax that with allergist input (Phase 1 Part B 13).

soy-lecithin.label: Soy lecithin
soy-lecithin.description: Soy lecithin emulsifier. Usually tolerated by people with soy allergy. The allergy module excludes it by default and lets the user relax that with allergist input (Phase 1 Part B 13).

lactose-high.label: Higher lactose
lactose-high.description: Dairy foods with a meaningful lactose load per usual serving: milk, ice cream, soft fresh cheeses, cream, condensed and evaporated milk, whey, milk powder, buttermilk. Lactose intolerance is dose-dependent; most people tolerate about 12 g (one cup of milk) at a time, so this is a limit, not an exclusion.

lactose-low.label: Lower lactose, usually tolerated
lactose-low.description: Dairy foods with little lactose per serving: hard aged cheeses, butter, ghee, yogurt with live cultures, kefir, lactose-free milk. Still milk for allergy purposes.

lactose-hidden.label: Hidden lactose
lactose-hidden.description: Non-dairy-looking foods that commonly contain lactose as an ingredient or filler: bread, processed meats, salad dressings, instant potatoes, and the ingredient 'lactose' itself.

added-sugar.label: Added sugar
added-sugar.description: A sugar or syrup added during processing, under any of its label names (sucrose, dextrose, corn syrup, cane juice, agave, honey, and so on), per the FDA Added Sugars definition.

sugar-sweetened-beverage.label: Sugar-sweetened beverage
sugar-sweetened-beverage.description: Beverage sweetened with added sugar: soda, sweet tea, energy and sports drinks, fruit punch, lemonade, sweetened coffee drinks. The largest single source of added sugar and the first thing to cut.

non-nutritive-sweetener.label: Non-nutritive or low-calorie sweetener
non-nutritive-sweetener.description: Non-sugar sweeteners covered by the WHO 2023 guideline (aspartame, sucralose, saccharin, acesulfame K, stevia, monk fruit) plus sugar alcohols (erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol, mannitol), which WHO's guideline does not cover but which the sugar module shows for awareness.

fodmap-fructan.label: FODMAP: fructans
fodmap-fructan.description: Fructo-oligosaccharide (fructan) source: wheat, rye, barley, onion, garlic, leek, shallot, artichoke, inulin, chicory root, FOS. Classification from published Monash-group composition studies, not the Monash app.

fodmap-gos.label: FODMAP: galacto-oligosaccharides
fodmap-gos.description: GOS source: legumes (chickpea, lentil, kidney bean, black bean, soybean), cashew, pistachio. GOS is water-soluble, so canned, rinsed legumes carry less.

fodmap-lactose.label: FODMAP: lactose
fodmap-lactose.description: Lactose-containing dairy restricted during FODMAP elimination. Overlaps with lactose-high; when both modules are on, the FODMAP rule governs (Phase 1 Part A 5).

fodmap-fructose.label: FODMAP: excess fructose
fodmap-fructose.description: Fructose in excess of glucose: honey, apple, pear, mango, watermelon, asparagus, high-fructose corn syrup, agave.

fodmap-sorbitol.label: FODMAP: sorbitol
fodmap-sorbitol.description: Sorbitol source: apple, pear, apricot, peach, nectarine, plum, prune, blackberry, avocado, sugar-free gum and candy.

fodmap-mannitol.label: FODMAP: mannitol
fodmap-mannitol.description: Mannitol source: mushroom, cauliflower, snow pea, celery, sweet potato, and mannitol as an ingredient.

histamine-high.label: Histamine: high or commonly reported trigger
histamine-high.description: Food with high measured histamine (scombroid fish, aged cheese, fermented and cured foods) or a commonly patient-reported trigger (tomato, spinach, eggplant, avocado, citrus, strawberry, chocolate, certain nuts). Patient-reported and food-chemistry basis; not RCT-confirmed; freshness and storage matter more than the food name.

histamine-fermented.label: Histamine: fermented
histamine-fermented.description: Fermentation-derived food or drink in which bacteria form histamine: alcohol, vinegar, sauerkraut, kimchi, kombucha, soy sauce, miso, fish sauce, fermented sausage. Patient-reported and food-chemistry basis; not RCT-confirmed.

histamine-aged.label: Histamine: aged or cured
histamine-aged.description: Aged cheese and cured, dried, or smoked meat and fish, where histamine accumulates with time. Patient-reported and food-chemistry basis; not RCT-confirmed; freshness and storage matter more than the food name.

phosphate-additive.label: Phosphate additive
phosphate-additive.description: Inorganic phosphate added in processing (any 'phos' ingredient, colas, processed cheese). Nearly fully absorbed, unlike plant phosphorus; KDOQI and KDIGO prioritize avoiding these over restricting natural phosphorus.

potassium-additive.label: Potassium additive
potassium-additive.description: Potassium salts added in processing (potassium chloride, citrate, lactate, bicarbonate, phosphate; salt substitutes). Fully absorbed. Matters when serum potassium is high.

potassium-high-food.label: High-potassium whole food
potassium-high-food.description: Classic high-potassium foods clinicians list (banana, orange, potato, tomato, spinach, avocado, dried fruit, beans, dairy milk, salt substitute). Restrict only when serum potassium is high, per KDIGO/KDOQI; plant potassium is less bioavailable. The app never sets a potassium limit itself.

oxalate-high.label: High oxalate
oxalate-high.description: High-oxalate food (spinach, rhubarb, almonds, beets, chard, okra, sweet potato, chocolate, bran, nuts, soy foods, black tea). Pairing rule: eat with a calcium source in the same meal rather than eliminating; do not restrict calcium (AUA).

purine-high.label: Purine: high
purine-high.description: Organ meats, anchovies, sardines, herring, mackerel, shellfish, game, gravies, yeast extract, beer. Limit per ACR 2020; diet is an adjunct, urate-lowering therapy is the treatment.

purine-moderate.label: Purine: moderate
purine-moderate.description: Beef, pork, lamb, poultry, and most finfish. Moderate intake per ACR 2020 framing. Purine-rich vegetables and legumes are not tagged: they did not raise gout risk in cohort data.

unpasteurized.label: Unpasteurized dairy or juice
unpasteurized.description: Raw milk, unpasteurized juice and cider, and soft cheeses that are often made from unpasteurized milk (brie, camembert, feta, blue, queso fresco). Listeria risk. Soft cheese entries carry the note 'unless labeled pasteurized'.

raw-animal.label: Raw or undercooked animal food
raw-animal.description: Raw or undercooked meat, fish, shellfish, and egg, and foods made with them (sushi with raw fish, raw oysters, tartare, ceviche, cookie dough, homemade mayonnaise, hollandaise). Salmonella, Toxoplasma, Listeria, Vibrio risk.

deli-meat.label: Deli meat, hot dogs, refrigerated smoked seafood
deli-meat.description: Ready-to-eat deli and luncheon meats, hot dogs, pate and meat spreads, and refrigerated smoked seafood (lox). Listeria risk; safe when heated until steaming hot.

mercury-high.label: Fish to avoid for mercury
mercury-high.description: FDA/EPA 2021 'Choices to Avoid': shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish (Gulf of Mexico), bigeye tuna, orange roughy, marlin.

mercury-low-fish.label: Low-mercury fish (Best Choices)
mercury-low-fish.description: FDA/EPA 2021 'Best Choices' list (2 to 3 servings a week): salmon, sardine, tilapia, cod, shrimp, canned light tuna, pollock, catfish, trout, and others. 'Good Choices' (1 serving a week) are noted but not tagged; see proposed_tags.

raw-sprouts.label: Raw sprouts
raw-sprouts.description: Raw alfalfa, clover, radish, mung bean, and other sprouts. Salmonella and E. coli risk; cooked sprouts are fine.

alcohol.label: Alcohol
alcohol.description: Alcoholic beverage or ingredient. None in pregnancy (ACOG). Also used by the gout rule (beer and spirits), the migraine diary, and the histamine trial.

caffeine.label: Caffeine source
caffeine.description: Coffee, espresso, black and green tea, energy drinks, cola, chocolate, yerba mate, guarana. Under 200 mg/day in pregnancy (ACOG); consistent intake for migraine.

vegetable.label: Vegetable
vegetable.description: Vegetable food group. Used by prefer rules in DASH, Mediterranean, diabetes, and gut-health patterns.

fruit.label: Fruit
fruit.description: Whole fruit food group. Juice and juice concentrate are not tagged fruit.

whole-grain.label: Whole grain
whole-grain.description: Whole grain: oats, brown rice, quinoa, whole wheat, barley, bulgur, farro, buckwheat, millet, and so on.

refined-grain.label: Refined grain
refined-grain.description: Refined grain: white bread, white rice, regular pasta, flour tortilla, enriched flour products.

legume.label: Legume
legume.description: Beans, peas, lentils, chickpeas, soy foods, peanuts (botanically a legume; also tagged nut).

nut.label: Nut
nut.description: Tree nuts and peanuts as a food group (PREDIMED, food group).

seed.label: Seed
seed.description: Edible seeds: sesame, chia, flax, hemp, pumpkin, sunflower, poppy.

fish.label: Fish and seafood
fish.description: Finfish and seafood as a food group (Mediterranean and AHA patterns: at least twice a week). Shellfish and mollusks are counted here too.

poultry.label: Poultry
poultry.description: Chicken, turkey, duck, and other poultry.

red-meat.label: Red meat
red-meat.description: Unprocessed mammalian muscle meat: beef, pork, lamb, veal, venison, bison, goat (IARC definition).

processed-meat.label: Processed meat
processed-meat.description: Meat transformed by salting, curing, fermentation, or smoking: bacon, sausage, ham, hot dogs, salami, pepperoni, deli meat, jerky (IARC definition).

low-fat-dairy.label: Low-fat or fat-free dairy
low-fat-dairy.description: Skim and 1% milk, low-fat and nonfat yogurt, part-skim and reduced-fat cheese (DASH).

full-fat-dairy.label: Full-fat dairy
full-fat-dairy.description: Whole milk, cream, butter, ice cream, regular cheese.

olive-oil.label: Olive oil
olive-oil.description: Olive oil, especially extra virgin, the main fat of the Mediterranean pattern.

ultra-processed.label: Ultra-processed marker
ultra-processed.description: Marker ingredients of NOVA group 4: hydrogenated or interesterified oils, high-fructose corn syrup, invert sugar, maltodextrin, modified starch, flavors, colors, nitrites, BHA/BHT/TBHQ, MSG. A single marker means the product is ultra-processed; it does not by itself mean unsafe.

fried.label: Fried food
fried.description: Deep-fried foods and fried snack foods.

high-fiber-insoluble.label: High insoluble fiber
high-fiber-insoluble.description: Bran, popcorn, flaxseed, celery, and other insoluble-fiber-dense foods. Limited during gastroparesis and IBD flare.

small-particle-friendly.label: Small-particle friendly
small-particle-friendly.description: Foods that are already soft or easily mashed (ground meat, flaky fish, yogurt, mashed potato, applesauce, purees, smooth soups) per the small-particle diet trial.

fermented-live-culture.label: Fermented food with live cultures
fermented-live-culture.description: Yogurt and kefir with live cultures, raw sauerkraut, kimchi, unpasteurized miso, tempeh, natto, kombucha. Small RCT support for microbiome diversity.

large-particle.label: Large particle
large-particle.description: Whole nuts, seeds, popcorn, raw vegetables, whole corn kernels: not easily mashed with a fork; avoided on the small-particle diet.

skin-or-seed.label: Skins or seeds
skin-or-seed.description: Fruit and vegetable skins, small seeds (berries, cucumber, tomato), hulls. Avoided during IBD flare and on the small-particle diet.

raw-vegetable.label: Raw vegetable
raw-vegetable.description: Vegetables eaten raw (salad greens, slaw, crudites). Avoided during IBD flare and gastroparesis; cooked versions are fine.

tough-meat.label: Tough or fibrous meat
tough-meat.description: Steak, roasts, chops, jerky: fibrous meat that is hard to break down; ground meat is the swap.

bezoar-risk.label: Bezoar-forming food
bezoar-risk.description: Persimmon, orange membranes and pith, celery, coconut: fibrous foods linked to phytobezoar formation in gastroparesis (Phase 1 D7).

iron-supplement.label: Iron supplement
iron-supplement.description: Iron supplements and iron-containing multivitamins. Keep about 4 hours from levothyroxine (the usual advice; the ATA guideline calls the gap untested).

calcium-rich.label: Calcium-rich food or supplement
calcium-rich.description: Milk, yogurt, cheese, calcium-fortified foods, calcium carbonate or citrate supplements and antacids. Calcium supplements and antacids: about 4 hours from levothyroxine (the usual advice; untested per the ATA guideline). Calcium-rich food: take the tablet 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime.

high-fiber.label: High-fiber food or supplement
high-fiber.description: Bran, psyllium, inulin, flax, chia, fiber supplements. Case reports link fiber to lower levothyroxine absorption: take the tablet 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, and keep fiber supplements about 4 hours away (the usual advice).

coffee.label: Coffee
coffee.description: Coffee and espresso drinks. Coffee reduces levothyroxine absorption (ATA 2014): take the tablet with water 60 minutes before breakfast coffee, or at bedtime.

may-contain.label: May contain / shared facility
may-contain.description: Precautionary allergen statements. Applied as an avoid only when the person has chosen to exclude them.

chocolate.label: Chocolate and cocoa
chocolate.description: Optional trigger for GERD and migraine; also listed among patient-reported MCAS triggers.

citrus.label: Citrus
citrus.description: Optional GERD trigger; patient-reported MCAS trigger; histamine lists include citrus.

tomato.label: Tomato
tomato.description: Optional GERD trigger; also histamine-high in patient lists.

tea.label: Tea
tea.description: Tea reduces non-heme iron absorption; separate from iron-rich meals by 1 to 2 hours.

msg.label: MSG
msg.description: Optional migraine trigger toggle; evidence weak.

aspartame.label: Aspartame
aspartame.description: Optional migraine trigger toggle; evidence weak.

iron-rich.label: Iron-rich food
iron-rich.description: Heme and non-heme iron sources used by the iron-deficiency guidance.

vitamin-c-rich.label: Vitamin C-rich food
vitamin-c-rich.description: Pair with non-heme iron to improve absorption.

emulsifier-additive.label: Emulsifier additive
emulsifier-additive.description: Food emulsifiers the AGA IBD update suggests limiting in remission (carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate 80, carrageenan).

smoked-seafood-refrigerated.label: Refrigerated smoked seafood
smoked-seafood-refrigerated.description: Lox, nova, kippered, jerky-style smoked fish sold refrigerated; avoid in pregnancy unless cooked.

basic-ingredient.label: Plain ingredient
basic-ingredient.description: A recognized everyday ingredient that carries no restriction tag on its own (salt, water, spices, plain starches, common oils). Sodium and other nutrients still count through the food database; this tag only tells the checker the word is known.

grapefruit.label: Grapefruit
grapefruit.description: Grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville orange (often in marmalade), pomelo, and lime. Their furanocoumarins block the gut enzyme (CYP3A4) that clears many medicines, so blood levels rise. Sweet oranges such as navel and Valencia do not. Applies only when a medicine on the interaction list is taken.

sodium-high.label: High in salt
sodium-high.description: Foods and ingredients that USDA FoodData Central lists above 600 mg sodium per 100 g, the UK front-of-pack "high" cutoff for foods (more than 1.5 g salt per 100 g; salt is sodium times 2.5). As may_contain: the word covers kinds above and below that cutoff (for example cheese: parmesan above, ricotta below). A fact about the food, not advice: it matters only when the plan has a daily sodium limit, and then the app says to check the sodium on the Nutrition Facts label. Evidence for each word: docs/VERIFY-log.md, fix pass F4.
